screens.title: Custom Attributes and Reflection for Editor Tools
screens.narratorSegment: In larger Unity projects, you often need a way to attach extra information to your scripts so editor tools can read it and behave differently. Custom attributes are tiny, declarative markers you add to classes, fields, properties, or methods. Reflection is the runtime mechanism that reads those markers and lets editor scripts inspect types, read values, and adapt the Inspector or automation tools. Together they let you write data-driven editor features: validation rules, designer hints, or small picker UIs that save time. For example, you can mark a health field as important, then show a highlighted summary in a custom inspector that displays the description and current value. That same pattern scales to required tags, scene-path checks, or automatic asset pickers. In this lesson we focus on safe usage: defining an attribute class that inherits from System. Attribute, applying it with AttributeUsage, and writing a simple Editor script that uses FieldInfo, PropertyInfo, and GetCustomAttribute to report metadata. We'll also cover common mistakes like overusing Reflection at runtime, and how to pick the right BindingFlags to find the members you need. By the end you'll know how to create a simple validator attribute and wire an Editor script to surface useful warnings and info to designers.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to define and apply custom attributes in C#, inspect those attributes using Reflection, and write simple Unity Editor scripts that act on metadata. First, you will learn the pattern for creating an attribute class that inherits from System. Attribute and how AttributeUsage controls where the marker is allowed. Second, you'll practice applying attributes to fields and properties so designer-facing metadata is explicit and discoverable. Third, you will learn how Reflection exposes Type, FieldInfo, PropertyInfo and extension methods such as GetCustomAttribute to read attribute instances. Fourth, you'll use that knowledge to build an Editor validator that warns when a tagged field contains an invalid value, like a missing Unity tag. Each objective combines a definition, an example, and a short application so you can see both the code pattern and the practical editor behavior it enables. We'll also touch on performance and maintenance trade-offs to help you decide when attributes plus Reflection are the right tool for your editor workflow.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Safety
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond writing attribute classes and reading them, it's essential to practice where and when to use Reflection. You'll practice building an Editor script that iterates over fields and properties, checks for an attribute, and then displays contextual information. We will also emphasize safety: Reflection bypasses compile-time checks, so your editor code should validate member types before invoking getters or callers. In addition, you'll learn to avoid using Reflection inside frequent runtime loops because it has higher call overhead and can slow frame rates. Instead, cache reflection results during initialization, or reserve Reflection for Editor tools and one-off initialization tasks. Finally, you will try a hands-on validator: a RequiredTag attribute that ensures a string field contains a Unity tag. This combines attribute definition, proper AttributeUsage, FieldInfo access, and EditorGUILayout feedback. Practicing these patterns helps you build predictable, maintainable editor features without compromising runtime performance or refactorability.

Practice & Safety

Practice: Build a validator

screens.title: What is a Custom Attribute in C#?
screens.narratorSegment: A custom attribute is a small C# class that inherits from System. Attribute and serves as a declarative tag you attach to code elements. It does not run logic by itself; instead, it carries data or marks a member so other code — commonly editor scripts — can detect and react to it. You declare an attribute class and usually end its name with Attribute, though you can use a short form when applying it. AttributeUsage controls where the attribute is legal, whether it can appear multiple times, and whether it is inherited by derived classes. For example, an ImportantFieldAttribute might include a Description property. Designers can apply it to fields to explain why a value matters. A common misconception is thinking attributes execute code immediately; they don't. Attributes are metadata only — Reflection reads them and executes behavior based on their presence. Another subtle point is that attributes are best for declarative, stable metadata. If behavior is highly dynamic or performance-sensitive, prefer direct code. To practice, define an attribute class, apply it to a field, and then write an Editor script that queries that field's attributes. The key takeaway: attributes let you annotate intent clearly and keep runtime code separate from editor tooling logic. Where will you add a marker in your next component?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › What is a Custom Attribute?
What is a Custom Attribute?
Metadata classes that mark code elements for tools to read.
Definition

A class that inherits from System.Attribute and contains data or flags used by other code via Reflection.

When to use
  • - To annotate designer-facing fields with context or constraints.
  • - To mark members for validation, custom drawing, or automated tooling.
Common misconception

Attributes do not execute; they only provide information. Reflection or other code interprets them.

Key Takeaway

Use attributes to express intent and supply metadata that editor tools can read safely.

Analogy: sticky notes

Imagine placing a sticky note on a field that says why it matters. The Editor reads those notes and highlights fields for designers.

using System;

[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Field | AttributeTargets.Property)]
public class ImportantFieldAttribute : Attribute
{
  public string Description { get; private set; }
  public ImportantFieldAttribute(string description = "This field is important for game balance.")
  {
    Description = description;
  }
}
Example: an attribute with a Description property used to annotate fields.
Try this

Create a tiny attribute, apply it to a field in a component, then inspect via Reflection in an Editor script to confirm you can read the Description value.

screens.title: Applying Attributes in Unity Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Applying an attribute is straightforward, but choosing where and how to apply it affects tooling and inheritance. You write an attribute class, then place it above a field, property, or class using square brackets. AttributeUsage is important: it sets AttributeTargets to restrict where the attribute is legal, AllowMultiple to permit more than one instance, and Inherited to control whether derived types receive the attribute. For Unity, common targets are Field and Property. When you annotate a public field, Unity's serializer and the Inspector still work as usual; the attribute simply adds metadata. A practical pattern is to use attributes for designer hints or validation rules. For example, mark a playerTag string with a RequiredTag attribute. Then in the Editor script, only inspect fields with that attribute and act on strings. A common mistake is assuming private fields will be found by default — when using Reflection, specify the correct BindingFlags, such as Public | Instance or NonPublic | Instance, depending on your target. Also avoid AttributeUsage that allows multiple instances unless you purposely want repeated markers. The concrete flow: define attribute, apply on fields, write Editor code that filters members by GetCustomAttribute, and then sample values with FieldInfo. GetValue. That pattern keeps metadata close to the code it describes while centralizing tool behavior in editor scripts.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Applying Attributes
Apply attributes: quick process
Follow these steps to annotate members for editor tools.
1
Define Attribute class
Inherit System.Attribute and expose any descriptive properties you need.
2
Choose AttributeUsage
Set targets, AllowMultiple, and Inherited to match intended use.
3
Apply to fields/properties
Annotate designer-facing fields; attributes do not change serialization by themselves.
4
Reflect and act
Editor scripts find these members and present warnings, pickers, or custom UI.
Tip: Keep attributes small and declarative — move behavior into Editor code.
Example: RequiredTag on a field
[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Field, AllowMultiple = false, Inherited = true)]
public class RequiredTagAttribute : Attribute
{
}

public class Door : MonoBehaviour
{
  [RequiredTag]
  public string playerTag = "Player";
}
BindingFlags reminder

When you call GetFields, pass BindingFlags.Public | BindingFlags.Instance to retrieve public instance fields. Add NonPublic if you annotated private fields that Unity serializes.

screens.title: Reading Attributes with Reflection
screens.narratorSegment: Reflection lets you examine a type and its members at runtime. In an Editor context you typically get the component instance, call GetType to obtain its Type, and then use GetFields or GetProperties with appropriate BindingFlags to enumerate members. FieldInfo and PropertyInfo represent fields and properties; from them you can call GetCustomAttribute () to retrieve an attribute instance. Once you have the attribute, you can read its properties and also call FieldInfo. GetValue to show the current value in the Inspector. A concrete example from this chapter is an ImportantFieldAttribute with a Description. The Editor script iterates enemy fields, asks for ImportantFieldAttribute, and when present draws an EditorGUILayout. HelpBox showing the field name, description, and current value. A common mistake is calling GetFields without BindingFlags and getting fewer members than expected. Another is assuming GetCustomAttribute returns non-null — always check for null before accessing Description or calling GetValue. For learning, write the Editor loop: Type myType = myObj. GetType(); FieldInfo[] fields = myType. GetFields(BindingFlags. Public | BindingFlags. Instance); then for each field call field. GetCustomAttribute () and if not null call field. GetValue(myObj). That pattern is the core of attribute-driven editor features.

keyIdea.text: Get Type → GetFields/GetProperties with BindingFlags → GetCustomAttribute<T>() → read attribute data and member values.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Reading Attributes
Reflection workflow
Type discovery and member inspection pattern for Editor scripts
Steps
  1. Get the instance's Type via GetType().
  2. Call GetFields or GetProperties with proper BindingFlags.
  3. Call member.GetCustomAttribute<T>() and check for null.
  4. Read attribute data and call GetValue to obtain current member value.
// Editor pseudo-code
Enemy enemy = (Enemy)target;
Type enemyType = enemy.GetType();
FieldInfo[] fields = enemyType.GetFields(BindingFlags.Public | BindingFlags.Instance);
foreach (FieldInfo field in fields)
{
  ImportantFieldAttribute attr = field.GetCustomAttribute();
  if (attr != null)
  {
    var value = field.GetValue(enemy);
    // Draw summary or HelpBox with field.Name, attr.Description, value
  }
}
Misconception: Reflection returns runtime behavior automatically. It only exposes metadata; you still write the code that interprets it.
Concrete example

An ImportantFieldAttribute with a Description is detected and then an Editor shows a help box with the description and the current value to guide designers during tweaking.

Common mistake

Forgetting to check null after GetCustomAttribute or using wrong BindingFlags leads to missed attributes or null reference errors.

Pro tip: Cache FieldInfo[] for a component type rather than calling GetFields repeatedly in editor UI redraws.

screens.title: Editor Script Integration
screens.narratorSegment: To make attributes actionable in Unity, you place the logic in an Editor script inside an Editor folder. The common entry point is a class deriving from UnityEditor. Editor and tagged with [CustomEditor(typeof(YourComponent))]. Inside your override of OnInspectorGUI, you typically call DrawDefaultInspector to preserve Unity's standard fields, then add custom sections that reflect attribute data. The Editor gets the inspected target, casts it to the component type, and uses Reflection to find attributes on fields or properties. For each detected attribute you can draw a HelpBox, add validation warnings, or show custom UI such as a dropdown. The architecture separates concerns: attributes declare metadata; Editor scripts implement presentation and validation. This separation improves maintainability because metadata remains close to the data it describes while the Editor code centralizes presentation rules. A common pitfall is modifying component state without marking the object as dirty via EditorUtility. SetDirty; changes won't persist to the scene. Also be mindful of Unity's serialization model when reading private serialized fields — choose BindingFlags that include NonPublic when necessary. Architect your Editor scripts to be resilient: check member existence, handle exceptions, and cache reflection results to keep the Inspector responsive.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Editor Integration
CustomEditor workflow
Connect attributes to the Inspector using a dedicated Editor class.
Typical OnInspectorGUI
  1. Call DrawDefaultInspector to show standard fields.
  2. Retrieve the target instance and its Type.
  3. Enumerate members, detect attributes, and draw HelpBoxes or UI.
  4. Optionally change values and call SetDirty to persist changes.
[CustomEditor(typeof(Enemy))]
public class ImportantFieldDrawer : Editor
{
  public override void OnInspectorGUI()
  {
    DrawDefaultInspector();
    Enemy enemy = (Enemy)target;
    Type enemyType = enemy.GetType();
    FieldInfo[] fields = enemyType.GetFields(BindingFlags.Public | BindingFlags.Instance);
    // show HelpBoxes for fields with ImportantFieldAttribute
  }
}
Practical notes
  • Remember Editor scripts run only in the Editor and should live in an Editor folder.
  • Call EditorUtility.SetDirty when you change component values so the scene saves correctly.
  • Cache reflection results outside frequent UI redraws to keep Inspector responsive.
Pitfall

Changing scene data without SetDirty or proper undo handling can silently lose work.

screens.title: Practical Applications: Patterns and Examples
screens.narratorSegment: Attributes and Reflection unlock a range of practical editor features. Consider four common patterns. First, custom inspector layouts: attributes like ReadOnly or Range can be implemented by reading markers and drawing appropriate UI. Second, data validation: attributes such as MustBePositive or RequiredTag let the Editor surface warnings immediately, preventing designer errors. Third, automated tools: markers can drive asset pickers or dropdowns so designers have context-aware controls without manual wiring. Fourth, serialization helpers: while Unity has its own serialization rules, attributes plus Reflection can help build custom serializers for unusual data shapes, used sparingly. Compare these patterns carefully: inspector UI changes focus on presentation and developer ergonomics; validation prevents incorrect data entry; automated tools accelerate workflows; custom serialization changes persistence behavior and must be designed with care. A common misconception is that attributes automatically change serialization — they do not. You must implement any serialization behavior yourself or integrate with Unity's serialization A P I. Use attributes where they provide clear designer benefit and keep logic centralized in Editor code so runtime code remains fast and type-safe. Practical Applications: Patterns and Examples means use attributes for custom ui, validation, pickers, and sparingly for custom serialization — always implement behavior in editor code.. In practical terms, inspector enhancements, validation, automated pickers, and serialization helpers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Practical Applications
Practical Applications
Common attribute-driven editor patterns and when to choose each
Custom Inspector UI

Draw ReadOnly fields, buttons, or sliders based on attribute presence to improve designer ergonomics without rewriting components.

Validation

Mark fields with RequiredTag or MustBePositive and display warnings to prevent incorrect data entering scenes.

Automated Tools

Use attributes to drive pickers or dropdowns, e.g., ScenePath or AssetReference markers that present context-aware pickers in the Inspector.

Serialization Helpers

When Unity serialization is insufficient, attributes can help identify fields for a custom serializer run in Editor or during initialization.

Decision guide: prefer Editor-driven UI and validation; reserve runtime Reflection and custom serialization for initialization or tooling phases.

screens.title: Performance, Type Safety, and Maintenance Concerns
screens.narratorSegment: Reflection is powerful, but it carries trade-offs. The primary runtime concern is performance: Reflection involves type lookups and dynamic invocation that are slower than direct calls. That makes Reflection a poor choice for code that runs every frame, such as in Update. Instead, favor caching reflection results and using them only in Editor code or during initialization. Type safety is another concern: Reflection bypasses compile-time checks. Accessing a field by name or invoking methods dynamically can break at runtime if member names change. To mitigate this, prefer retrieving attribute instances by type rather than relying on string names, and write defensive checks for nulls and parameter mismatches. Maintenance costs rise when many behaviors depend on string-based reflection; refactorers and teammates may miss these hidden links. Also be careful with BindingFlags: forgetting to include NonPublic will miss private serialized fields, while overly broad flags can expose unintended members. Finally, wrap Reflection in utility helpers and document assumptions so future developers can maintain tools safely. In short, use Reflection for Editor tools, initialization tasks, or one-off automation — not for tight runtime loops.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Performance & Safety
Performance & Safety
Avoid common pitfalls when using Reflection in Unity
Performance

Reflection is slower than direct calls. Cache FieldInfo and attribute lookups and avoid calling them in Update or other frequent loops.

Type safety

Reflection bypasses compile-time checks. Verify member existence and types before calling GetValue or Invoke.

Maintenance

Relying on strings or implicit contracts increases refactor risk. Keep attribute contracts small and documented.

BindingFlags

Specify BindingFlags explicitly to include the members you need (Public/NonPublic, Static/Instance) and avoid surprises.

screens.title: BindingFlags and Member Discovery
screens.narratorSegment: BindingFlags control what GetFields, GetProperties, and similar Reflection calls return. Common flags include Public, NonPublic, Instance, Static, FlattenHierarchy, and DeclaredOnly. A typical Editor inspection uses BindingFlags. Public | BindingFlags. Instance to list public instance fields. If you annotated private serialized fields, add NonPublic. If your attribute target is on a base class and you want inherited members, be intentional about FlattenHierarchy or rely on Inherited in AttributeUsage. A subtle point: GetFields without explicit flags may return only public instance fields, depending on the runtime. Therefore always pass flags to avoid surprises. Another misconception is expecting GetFields to include properties; it does not — use GetProperties for those. When you design a validator, think through the exact members you need and test different flags in the Editor to ensure you spot all annotated members. For safe tooling, filter members by type when necessary, handle exceptions around GetValue and Invoke, and cache the final set of FieldInfo objects so subsequent UI draws are fast. Understanding BindingFlags prevents missed attributes and reduces bugs when extending your tooling to more complex components. fullNarratorScript:
In larger Unity projects, you often need a way to attach extra information to your scripts so editor tools can read it and behave differently. Custom attributes are tiny, declarative markers you add to classes, fields, properties, or methods. Reflection is the runtime mechanism that reads those markers and lets editor scripts inspect types, read values, and adapt the Inspector or automation tools. Together they let you write data-driven editor features: validation rules, designer hints, or small picker UIs that save time. For example, you can mark a health field as important, then show a highlighted summary in a custom inspector that displays the description and current value. That same pattern scales to required tags, scene-path checks, or automatic asset pickers. In this lesson we focus on safe usage: defining an attribute class that inherits from System. Attribute, applying it with AttributeUsage, and writing a simple Editor script that uses FieldInfo, PropertyInfo, and GetCustomAttribute to report metadata. We'll also cover common mistakes like overusing Reflection at runtime, and how to pick the right BindingFlags to find the members you need. By the end you'll know how to create a simple validator attribute and wire an Editor script to surface useful warnings and info to designers.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define and apply custom attributes in C#, inspect those attributes using Reflection, and write simple Unity Editor scripts that act on metadata. First, you will learn the pattern for creating an attribute class that inherits from System. Attribute and how AttributeUsage controls where the marker is allowed. Second, you'll practice applying attributes to fields and properties so designer-facing metadata is explicit and discoverable. Third, you will learn how Reflection exposes Type, FieldInfo, PropertyInfo and extension methods such as GetCustomAttribute to read attribute instances. Fourth, you'll use that knowledge to build an Editor validator that warns when a tagged field contains an invalid value, like a missing Unity tag. Each objective combines a definition, an example, and a short application so you can see both the code pattern and the practical editor behavior it enables. We'll also touch on performance and maintenance trade-offs to help you decide when attributes plus Reflection are the right tool for your editor workflow.

Beyond writing attribute classes and reading them, it's essential to practice where and when to use Reflection. You'll practice building an Editor script that iterates over fields and properties, checks for an attribute, and then displays contextual information. We will also emphasize safety: Reflection bypasses compile-time checks, so your editor code should validate member types before invoking getters or callers. In addition, you'll learn to avoid using Reflection inside frequent runtime loops because it has higher call overhead and can slow frame rates. Instead, cache reflection results during initialization, or reserve Reflection for Editor tools and one-off initialization tasks. Finally, you will try a hands-on validator: a RequiredTag attribute that ensures a string field contains a Unity tag. This combines attribute definition, proper AttributeUsage, FieldInfo access, and EditorGUILayout feedback. Practicing these patterns helps you build predictable, maintainable editor features without compromising runtime performance or refactorability.

A custom attribute is a small C# class that inherits from System. Attribute and serves as a declarative tag you attach to code elements. It does not run logic by itself; instead, it carries data or marks a member so other code — commonly editor scripts — can detect and react to it. You declare an attribute class and usually end its name with Attribute, though you can use a short form when applying it. AttributeUsage controls where the attribute is legal, whether it can appear multiple times, and whether it is inherited by derived classes. For example, an ImportantFieldAttribute might include a Description property. Designers can apply it to fields to explain why a value matters. A common misconception is thinking attributes execute code immediately; they don't. Attributes are metadata only — Reflection reads them and executes behavior based on their presence. Another subtle point is that attributes are best for declarative, stable metadata. If behavior is highly dynamic or performance-sensitive, prefer direct code. To practice, define an attribute class, apply it to a field, and then write an Editor script that queries that field's attributes. The key takeaway: attributes let you annotate intent clearly and keep runtime code separate from editor tooling logic. Where will you add a marker in your next component?

Applying an attribute is straightforward, but choosing where and how to apply it affects tooling and inheritance. You write an attribute class, then place it above a field, property, or class using square brackets. AttributeUsage is important: it sets AttributeTargets to restrict where the attribute is legal, AllowMultiple to permit more than one instance, and Inherited to control whether derived types receive the attribute. For Unity, common targets are Field and Property. When you annotate a public field, Unity's serializer and the Inspector still work as usual; the attribute simply adds metadata. A practical pattern is to use attributes for designer hints or validation rules. For example, mark a playerTag string with a RequiredTag attribute. Then in the Editor script, only inspect fields with that attribute and act on strings. A common mistake is assuming private fields will be found by default — when using Reflection, specify the correct BindingFlags, such as Public | Instance or NonPublic | Instance, depending on your target. Also avoid AttributeUsage that allows multiple instances unless you purposely want repeated markers. The concrete flow: define attribute, apply on fields, write Editor code that filters members by GetCustomAttribute, and then sample values with FieldInfo. GetValue. That pattern keeps metadata close to the code it describes while centralizing tool behavior in editor scripts.

Reflection lets you examine a type and its members at runtime. In an Editor context you typically get the component instance, call GetType to obtain its Type, and then use GetFields or GetProperties with appropriate BindingFlags to enumerate members. FieldInfo and PropertyInfo represent fields and properties; from them you can call GetCustomAttribute () to retrieve an attribute instance. Once you have the attribute, you can read its properties and also call FieldInfo. GetValue to show the current value in the Inspector. A concrete example from this chapter is an ImportantFieldAttribute with a Description. The Editor script iterates enemy fields, asks for ImportantFieldAttribute, and when present draws an EditorGUILayout. HelpBox showing the field name, description, and current value. A common mistake is calling GetFields without BindingFlags and getting fewer members than expected. Another is assuming GetCustomAttribute returns non-null — always check for null before accessing Description or calling GetValue. For learning, write the Editor loop: Type myType = myObj. GetType(); FieldInfo[] fields = myType. GetFields(BindingFlags. Public | BindingFlags. Instance); then for each field call field. GetCustomAttribute () and if not null call field. GetValue(myObj). That pattern is the core of attribute-driven editor features.

To make attributes actionable in Unity, you place the logic in an Editor script inside an Editor folder. The common entry point is a class deriving from UnityEditor. Editor and tagged with [CustomEditor(typeof(YourComponent))]. Inside your override of OnInspectorGUI, you typically call DrawDefaultInspector to preserve Unity's standard fields, then add custom sections that reflect attribute data. The Editor gets the inspected target, casts it to the component type, and uses Reflection to find attributes on fields or properties. For each detected attribute you can draw a HelpBox, add validation warnings, or show custom UI such as a dropdown. The architecture separates concerns: attributes declare metadata; Editor scripts implement presentation and validation. This separation improves maintainability because metadata remains close to the data it describes while the Editor code centralizes presentation rules. A common pitfall is modifying component state without marking the object as dirty via EditorUtility. SetDirty; changes won't persist to the scene. Also be mindful of Unity's serialization model when reading private serialized fields — choose BindingFlags that include NonPublic when necessary. Architect your Editor scripts to be resilient: check member existence, handle exceptions, and cache reflection results to keep the Inspector responsive.

Attributes and Reflection unlock a range of practical editor features. Consider four common patterns. First, custom inspector layouts: attributes like ReadOnly or Range can be implemented by reading markers and drawing appropriate UI. Second, data validation: attributes such as MustBePositive or RequiredTag let the Editor surface warnings immediately, preventing designer errors. Third, automated tools: markers can drive asset pickers or dropdowns so designers have context-aware controls without manual wiring. Fourth, serialization helpers: while Unity has its own serialization rules, attributes plus Reflection can help build custom serializers for unusual data shapes, used sparingly. Compare these patterns carefully: inspector UI changes focus on presentation and developer ergonomics; validation prevents incorrect data entry; automated tools accelerate workflows; custom serialization changes persistence behavior and must be designed with care. A common misconception is that attributes automatically change serialization — they do not. You must implement any serialization behavior yourself or integrate with Unity's serialization A P I. Use attributes where they provide clear designer benefit and keep logic centralized in Editor code so runtime code remains fast and type-safe. Practical Applications: Patterns and Examples means use attributes for custom ui, validation, pickers, and sparingly for custom serialization — always implement behavior in editor code.. In practical terms, inspector enhancements, validation, automated pickers, and serialization helpers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reflection is powerful, but it carries trade-offs. The primary runtime concern is performance: Reflection involves type lookups and dynamic invocation that are slower than direct calls. That makes Reflection a poor choice for code that runs every frame, such as in Update. Instead, favor caching reflection results and using them only in Editor code or during initialization. Type safety is another concern: Reflection bypasses compile-time checks. Accessing a field by name or invoking methods dynamically can break at runtime if member names change. To mitigate this, prefer retrieving attribute instances by type rather than relying on string names, and write defensive checks for nulls and parameter mismatches. Maintenance costs rise when many behaviors depend on string-based reflection; refactorers and teammates may miss these hidden links. Also be careful with BindingFlags: forgetting to include NonPublic will miss private serialized fields, while overly broad flags can expose unintended members. Finally, wrap Reflection in utility helpers and document assumptions so future developers can maintain tools safely. In short, use Reflection for Editor tools, initialization tasks, or one-off automation — not for tight runtime loops.
